sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Open source is a copyright licence, not a free-for-all
sections.para: Common misconceptions are corrected: a few maintainers control what goes in, most projects are run by a handful of people, security depends on paid review time, somebody always pays, open weights are a compiled binary, and no licence means all rights reserved. The real power of open source is that nobody can lock you in.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Open source is licensed control, with no lock-in
sections.para: An open source licence uses copyright to grant copying, use and change; it began as the GPL's copyleft, reframed as open source in 1998. Maintainers control what goes in, security depends on review time and money, and somebody always pays. The point is the freedom to read, run, fix and move software.

sections.label: A copyright licence, from copyleft to open source
sections.line: From GPL copyleft to open source, still a licence
sections.para: Stallman's GPL, first released in 1989, made sharing a condition, and Christine Peterson proposed open source in February 1998 as Perens and Raymond founded the OSI. Linux adopted GPL version 2 in 1992 and stayed. Apache 2.0 adds a patent grant, and having no licence means all rights reserved.

sections.label: Misconception one: anybody can change it, so nobody controls it
sections.line: A few maintainers decide; the control is simply visible
sections.para: Serious projects have one or a handful of maintainers who review, test, sign off and often refuse contributions, recording provenance through certificates or contributor agreements. Anybody can fork and change their own copy, but nobody can change yours without you. Visible control is a strength.

sections.label: Misconception two: open source means anybody contributes
sections.line: Most open source projects are run by few people
sections.para: The barrier to contributing is lower than for proprietary software, which often cannot even be built. But apart from a very small minority of very popular projects, most are run by a small number of people. Expecting a large community leads people to miss what is actually there.

sections.label: Misconception three: it is more, or less, secure
sections.line: Security depends on paid review time, not on openness
sections.para: Open source is neither much more nor less secure than proprietary software. What matters is whether someone had the time, usually paid, to review and test it, and how widely it is used. Black Duck finds open source in almost all commercial codebases, so closing a product only hides its dependencies.

sections.label: Misconception four: it is free, so it costs nothing
sections.line: Open source is not free: somebody is always paying
sections.para: Tidelift's 2024 survey found around 60% of maintainers call themselves unpaid hobbyists, and paid ones follow more security practices. The xz utils backdoor of March 2024 hit a library maintained by one person with no time or money. Maintainers should be paid, and agents may finally make the workflows practical.

sections.label: Misconception five: open weights are open source
sections.line: Open weights are a compiled binary, not open source
sections.para: Weights can be run and fine-tuned but not rebuilt, so labs are right to say open weights. The OSI's Open Source AI Definition requires training code, parameters and enough data information to build an equivalent system. Open weights remain a large economic advantage, just a different thing.

sections.label: Misconception six: openness is the danger
sections.line: What matters is how a tool is used
sections.para: Fear about open-weight models echoes past worries; Metasploit made exploitation easier and the world adjusted. Some highly destructive capabilities should not be released, and some technology will be controlled. Hosting and distribution are themselves points of control, so open source is never a free-for-all.

sections.label: What open source is for
sections.line: The power of open source is freedom from lock-in
sections.para: Not contributions but the ability to read, run, fix and move software, even if its company is sold or disappears, plus the whole development workflow with history, tests and builds. That is why there is no sovereignty without it. open-source.sgit.ai's first lesson: open source is not free.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Not legal advice; history shortened; figures are surveys
sections.para: Licences are legal instruments, so read them and ask a lawyer. Earlier permissive licences existed alongside the GPL, with the fuller story on open-source.sgit.ai. Tidelift's 60% is self-description, and contributions do happen; the claim is only that they are not the point or the norm.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: OSI, choosealicense, Black Duck, Tidelift and Wikipedia
sections.para: A voice memo of 12 October 2026, with history corrected from sources. The Open Source Initiative and open-source.sgit.ai's timeline, choosealicense.com, Black Duck's OSSRA, Tidelift's 2024 maintainer report via The Register, the Open Source AI Definition, and Wikipedia on the xz case.
